h2: Liquid penetrant testing myths that hide real indications
html:
Liquid penetrant testing myths that hide real indications

Penetrant testing fails quietly. A missed crack leaves no trace on the report, so the mistakes below rarely get noticed until something leaks or breaks. Most happen in the removal, development and interpretation steps rather than in the penetrant itself. Myths across all five conventional methods are in conventional NDT myths.

Myth: Spraying remover straight onto the part removes excess penetrant faster

It also removes penetrant from shallow flaws. With the solvent-removable method, excess penetrant is wiped off with a clean, dry, lint-free cloth, then with a cloth dampened with remover, until no color remains on the surface; the National Board describes the same sequence. Flushing the surface with solvent washes penetrant out of exactly the tight, shallow cracks the examination is for, which is why code procedures forbid it. When a field technician is in a hurry, this is the step where indications disappear.

Myth: A thicker developer coat shows more

Developer works as a thin, even, white film that draws penetrant out of the flaw and gives contrast. Laid on thick, it hides fine indications instead, because the bleed-out from a tight crack cannot reach the surface of a heavy coat. The National Board calls for a thin, light coating, applied as the manufacturer and procedure direct. Shake aerosol cans well, spray from the distance printed on the can, and build up light passes rather than one wet one.

Myth: Grinding or blasting first gives PT a cleaner surface

Mechanical surface work can close the flaws PT is meant to find. Grinding, sanding, power wire brushing and shot or grit blasting drag metal over the mouths of cracks, and that smeared layer must be removed before testing. Aluminum, copper alloys and other soft metals smear most readily. Where mechanical work was unavoidable, aerospace and other critical-part specifications commonly call for etching under a controlled procedure before PT. Clean with solvents or detergents wherever you can, and record what was done to the surface.

Myth: You can read indications any time after the developer dries

The procedure sets an interpretation window for a reason. Read too early and slow-bleeding indications have not appeared; read too late and bleed-out spreads, so an indication looks bigger than the flaw and an acceptable indication can become rejectable. The National Board makes the same point. Watch the surface as the developer dries, note where indications start, and make the final evaluation within the time the procedure allows.

Myth: A hard rinse gives a cleaner background

With water-washable penetrant, an aggressive rinse over-washes: it pulls penetrant out of wide, shallow flaws along with the background. Procedures limit water pressure and temperature and call for a coarse spray at an angle. In a factory wash station using fluorescent penetrant, the rinse is checked under UV-A light so the operator stops when the background is gone, not later. Post-emulsifiable systems exist for parts where over-washing is a known risk, because the emulsifier contact time controls what is removed.

Myth: If visible dye shows nothing, look again with fluorescent penetrant

Not on the same surface. Red dye left in a flaw interferes with the fluorescence of a later Type I penetrant, so most penetrant specifications forbid a fluorescent examination after a visible-dye examination of the same area. Choose the system before you start: fluorescent penetrant inspection (FPI) for fine cracks and much aerospace work, visible dye for field welds in daylight. Mixing penetrant, remover and developer from different families or makers breaks the system the procedure qualified, so keep each system together. Related pages: PT of welds, PT of stainless steel, penetrant testing training, the PT simulator and NDT procedure development.
